readerTitle: You have two planes. Where do you fly them?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (신생 지역 항공사, 지역 철물·건축자재 매장) · 실제 기업 수치 없음
insight: 신생 사업의 전략은 '수요가 가장 큰 곳'이 아니라 '이길 수 있는 곳'을 먼저 고르고, 그 자리를 지키기 위해 무엇을 포기할지 정하는 일이다.
misconception: 작은 신생 회사도 가장 큰 시장에 들어가 더 많은 고객 요구를 들어줄수록 성공 확률이 높아진다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨 STR-01-04 (Where to play, how to win), STR-01-05 (Trade-offs)
모든 사례와 상황은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 항공사·매장 사례는 가상입니다. 실제 항공사 이름, 노선, 통계는 쓰지 않았습니다. '5시간 운전' 등 수치도 설명용 가정입니다.
STR-01-06(Southwest, 활동 간 적합성)과 겹치지 않도록 단일 기종·턴어라운드 이야기는 넣지 않았습니다. 게시 전 STR-01-04, STR-01-05 본문과 용어 정의가 일치하는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: You have two planes. Where do you fly them?
body: Dana spent fifteen years running ground operations at a regional airport. Now she has leased two small jets and raised enough money for about eighteen months.
On her desk is a list of forty possible routes. Two planes can fly maybe four of them well. Every choice she makes in the next month will decide whether her airline lives past year two.

image.label: A founder at a desk with a route map and two toy planes
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 책상 위에 지역 노선 지도가 펼쳐져 있고, 작은 비행기 모형 두 대가 놓여 있음. 지도에는 수많은 점선 노선, 그중 몇 개에만 손가락이 닿아 있음. 실제 항공사 로고나 도장은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which routes should Dana start with?
body: The busiest route in the region links the capital and the biggest city. Three large airlines already fly it many times a day.
Several mid-size cities have no direct flights between them. People drive about five hours or connect through a hub.

options.text: The busiest route. That's where the most passengers are
options.feedback: Big demand, but big rivals with more flights, lounges and loyalty points. With two planes, Dana has no way to win there. Where you play has to match how you can win.

options.text: The mid-size city pairs with no direct flight
options.feedback: Smaller markets, but Dana's real competitor is a five-hour drive, and she can beat that. This is where to play, how to win: pick the field where your advantage counts.

options.text: Fly ten routes a few times a week and see what works
options.feedback: Testing sounds safe, but two planes spread over ten routes means flights too rare to be useful. She learns slowly and wins nowhere.

cards.title: From "where's the demand?" to "where can we win?"
body: Dana picks three city pairs. Now she can say how she'll win there: a **direct flight, timed for a day trip**. Out at 7 a.m., back at 6 p.m., at a fare close to the cost of driving and a hotel night.

That answer shapes everything else. Her schedule serves business day-trippers, not vacationers. Her marketing targets companies in those cities, not the whole country. A clear where-to-play makes the how-to-win concrete.

image.label: Map with three highlighted direct routes between mid-size cities
image.brief: 지역 지도 인포그래픽. 큰 허브 공항 하나에 굵은 노선이 몰려 있고(회색), 중소 도시 세 쌍을 잇는 직항 노선 세 개만 밝은 색으로 강조. 옆에 작은 시계 아이콘 "7:00 out / 18:00 back". 실제 지명은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: An investor wants a premium cabin.
body: Six months in, flights are filling up. An investor points out that business travelers would pay much more for wider seats and a hot meal. Adding a premium cabin would remove 12 regular seats per plane.

options.text: Add the premium cabin on every flight
options.feedback: She gains high fares but loses seats, adds catering and raises the cost of every regular ticket. Her day-trip fare stops beating the drive. Trade-offs cut both ways.

options.text: Keep one cabin, and sell a flexible fare business travelers can upgrade to
options.feedback: She gives up some premium revenue to keep seats cheap, which is her reason to exist. Picking one side of a trade-off is what makes a position hard to copy.

options.text: Add premium seats only on Monday morning flights
options.feedback: It targets the right moment, but now two plane layouts, swapping, and crews trained for both. She pays the cost of both choices in a smaller way.

cards.title: Saying no to good money can protect the business.
body: The premium cabin wasn't a bad idea. It was a good idea for a different airline. That's what a **trade-off** looks like: more of one thing means less of another. Here, space per passenger versus seats per plane.
Big rivals face the same trade-off in reverse. To match Dana's fares, they would have to strip out the premium seats their best customers pay for. So they usually don't.
cards.softwareNote: A new software company faces this when one large client asks for custom features. Saying yes brings revenue but makes the product slower and harder to use for the hundreds of small customers it was built for.

cards.title: Clear choices can still be wrong.
body: Choosing where to play is a bet, not a fact. If a big airline adds a direct flight on one of Dana's routes, her how-to-win must still hold. Can she stay cheaper or better timed? If not, the route is no longer hers.

And every trade-off has a real price. The premium fares she turned down are money she will never see. Review your choices on a schedule, and change them when the facts change, not when one investor gets impatient.

cards.title: Now it's a hardware store.
body: You're opening a building-supply and hardware store in a growing town. A big-box home store sits 20 minutes away with a huge range and low prices. Many local contractors start work at 6 a.m. and lose time driving there.
Which plan gives you the best chance?

options.text: Match the big-box store on range and price, closer to town
options.feedback: You'd fight on the rival's strongest ground with less buying power. A smaller version of the leader rarely wins.

options.text: Serve contractors: open at 5:30, stock their core items in depth, deliver to job sites
options.feedback: A clear where to play (contractors) and how to win (time saved). The trade-off: you give up weekend browsers and decor, and that focus is what makes the plan work.

options.text: Serve everyone, and add delivery as an extra
options.feedback: Delivery helps, but stocking for everyone means thin shelves on what contractors need. Without a trade-off, there's no clear reason to choose you.

cards.softwareNote: The same logic fits a new app against a market leader: pick the users the leader serves badly, and accept that the app won't do everything.

cards.title: Pick the field you can win, then guard it.
body: Two ideas did the work here. **Where to play, how to win** moved Dana from the busiest route to routes she could win. **Trade-offs** helped her turn down a premium cabin that would have weakened her fares. The hardware store used both.
**Try it today:** write one sentence: "We serve ___, and we win because ___." Then list one profitable request you would turn down to protect it.
